title: The 227 rules
hookLine: a fully ordained monk keeps 227 rules, a nun more; rules as a shelter

cards: Rules are complicated. Speed limits, dress codes, the terms and conditions nobody reads. Rules can feel like a fence someone else built around you.
A Theravada monk chooses, freely, to live by two hundred twenty-seven of them. Not eating after noon. Not touching money.
Not digging in the ground. Not sleeping in a luxurious bed. That's the life of a fully ordained monk, and some keep it their whole lives.
Why would anyone want that? The tradition's answer changes what a rule is.

teach.b: Vinaya means discipline, or training. It's the first of the three baskets.
At its center is a list called the Pāṭimokkha: two hundred twenty-seven rules for monks in the Theravada tradition, and three hundred eleven for fully ordained nuns.

teach.h: FOUR DEFEATS AND MANY SMALL RULES.
teach.b: Four are the gravest, called defeats: sexual intercourse, stealing, killing a human being, and falsely claiming spiritual attainments. Break one and you're no longer a monk.
Most of the rest are small, and many have wonderful origin stories. The rule against digging the ground exists because of the small creatures living in the soil.

teach.h: RECITED AT EVERY NEW AND FULL MOON.
teach.b: Every two weeks, on the new moon and the full moon, the monks of a monastery gather, confess any lapses to each other, and one of them recites the whole list aloud.

The Vinaya gives the Buddha's own reasons for making rules, ten of them, including the well-being of the community, its ease, restraint for the difficult, and the confidence of people who see monks living well.

So the rules work less like a fence and more like a shelter: they keep the weather out so the practice can happen inside. About nuns: in Sri Lanka the Theravada line of fully ordained nuns died out centuries ago.
In recent decades, ordinations have revived it, and some Sri Lankan and Western Theravadins recognize those nuns. The official monastic councils of Thailand and Myanmar do not yet.
Look back at the week: one hand, carry it, just sitting, the way of the elders, three baskets, the forest remembers.

how: Theravada monks keep the 227 rules of the Pāṭimokkha, confess lapses to one another and recite the rules together every new and full moon; lay Buddhists keep five precepts, and eight on observance days.

games.q: a monk wants to plant a vegetable garden behind the monastery. which rule stops him from digging the bed himself?
o: the rule against digging the ground, for the creatures in the soil.
games.why: monks don't dig the ground themselves because of the small creatures in the soil; lay helpers often do it instead.

practice: Choose one small rule just for yourself, nothing heroic: no phone at the table, no second helping, not interrupting, no complaining until noon.
Picture it not as a fence but as a small roof over your day, keeping something out so something else can grow, and breathe under that roof.

wordCard.voice: Vinaya. The monastic discipline: two hundred twenty-seven rules for Theravada monks, kept as a shelter for practice.

orig.note: Pali and Sanskrit vinaya: discipline, training.

carryVoice: Your line: rules as a shelter. Weather stays out, practice grows in. That's the week.
